name: Coiling vine
description:
One cord that left one point and wound twice round the circle the weapon catches in. It is a helix seen from above: the radius opens as it climbs, because a coil of even radius is a hoop and a hoop is not something that grew, and the far end sits nine pixels above the near one so the two turns do not print on top of each other. It thins from four and a half to under one along its length and ends in a fiddlehead, the tight curl a vine carries at its growing end. One short branch leaves it just past halfway and winds the other way — short, because a branch that rivals its own trunk is two plants.

**The shape is the path it grew along, and that is the whole point of this document.** Three earlier versions had a shape that simply sat there and an arrival bolted on afterwards: a mound of soil thrown up at the centre, then a longer climb, then a neck grafted on to give the thing somewhere to come up from. Every fix made the drawing worse, because the drawing was never the problem — a plant whose shape is not the path it grew along has no animation in it to find. Here the cord is cut into nine segments in the order it travels — one per frame of the baked sheet, which is the only ratio at which every step of the growth is a picture somebody actually sees, each one held relative to its own start, which is the end of the one before it. So `coil` is nothing more than revealing them in that order: root first, tip last, each rising out of the floor while turning on its own joint. Because that joint is its parent's end, a turning segment sweeps out of the segment that made it rather than appearing beside it, and the windows are sequenced rather than overlapped so the chain is never drawn broken. The root comes up furthest — it is the part actually leaving the ground — and by the tip the cord is winding rather than climbing.

Dark all through: `$moss.dark2` with a `$moss` lit edge and `$blood.dark2` thorns, a dark red against a dark green, which is the one pairing that keeps a barb readable at this size without lightening the plant. Thorns hang on the segment they grow from and turn with it. No leaves — a coil hung with foliage stops being a cord. `meta.radius` is the circle the cord winds round, which is the circle the weapon catches in.

coil.description: coil — the cord comes up at the root and winds round, segment by segment

evolved.description: Gold along the cord's lit edge and on the thorns, the mark every evolution in this arsenal wears. The body stays dark: a coil gilded through stops reading as a growing thing, and what the evolution changed is the grip, not the plant.

slot.description:
The slot ramp. A 32px icon and a sprite on the field are lit for different jobs: the field wants a cord that stays out of the way of a crowd, and the slot wants something legible at a tenth of the area with nothing around it to read against. Two ramp steps up on each of the drawing's three colours — cord to `$moss`, lit edge to `$lichen`, thorns to `$blood` — with the field sprite untouched.

One step was tried first and was not enough, and the way that was found is worth keeping: the slot was laid out beside the other seven weapons rather than looked at on its own. Every one of them is a bright glyph on a dark plate — a white moon, a bile glob, husk mandibles — and the vine was a dark cord on a dark plate. It did not read as a weapon with a colour, it read as the slot that had not been finished yet. That comparison is the only way to judge an icon, because a row is where one is actually seen.

Brightening the *backdrop* instead was the obvious alternative and is the wrong one: the cord is already darker than the plate behind it, and lifting the plate toward it takes contrast off the very thing the slot is of.

evolved-slot.description: The evolved plant on the slot ramp — `evolved` and `slot` both, because a variant is a patch rather than a stack and the evolved icon would otherwise drop back to the field's darkness the moment it gilded.
